sn36.11:2.1: The Buddha praises the mendicant because he had the critical acumen to notice these apparently different explanations, and, rather than assuming they were contradictory, or just ignoring the problem, he asked the Buddha for clarification. Compare the Buddha’s quite different response at [sn36.19:5.1]().
sn36.11:2.15: The “progressive cessation of activities” (_anupubbasaṅkhārānaṁ nirodho_), and their “settling” (_vūpasama_) and “tranquilizing” (_passaddhi_) are only mentioned here, [sn36.15](), and [sn36.17](). Compare the nine “progressive cessations” of [an9.31]() and [dn33:3.2.82](), but these go even further to full enlightenment, as in the “progressive cessation in a definitive sense” at [an9.61](). | “Activities” (_saṅkhārā_) are the conditioned phenomena that are active, being both produced by and productive of other conditions. Here they are the “processes” that are stilled in the course of meditation.
sn36.11:2.31: This is the same at the corresponding point in [sn36.17:2.7](), but at  [sn36.15:1.22]() it speaks of the “progressive tranquilizing of activities”.
